findings.title: Webhook endpoint does not verify signatures
findings.description: The receive_webhook endpoint (lines 357-409) accepts POST requests to /api/hooks/{session_id} without verifying webhook signatures. While the code reads GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET from environment (line 66), it is never used to verify incoming webhook signatures. This means ANYONE can send fake webhook payloads to the public URL.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker discovers the public HookRelay URL (e.g., from Cloudflare tunnel or permanent hostname). 2. Attacker sends a forged POST request to /api/hooks/stripe with a fake payment.captured event. 3. HookRelay saves the fake event to PostgreSQL and forwards it to the local app. 4. Local app processes the fake event, potentially triggering business logic based on fraudulent data. 5. For GitHub webhooks, attacker can trigger repository actions by sending fake push events.
findings.impact: Complete trust failure in webhook data. Payment integrations (Stripe, Razorpay) are fully compromisable - attackers can fake successful payments, trigger order fulfillment, or corrupt business data. GitHub webhooks can be forged to trigger CI/CD or other automated workflows. Attackers can replay, modify, or invent webhook payloads at will.
findings.recommendation: Implement HMAC signature verification in receive_webhook function. For GitHub: validate X-Hub-Signature-256 header using the webhook secret. For Stripe: validate Stripe-Signature header. Add middleware or decorator that verifies signatures BEFORE processing the request. Example: if not verify_signature(request.headers, request.body, secret): raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid signature")
findings.playbook: 1. Revoke any webhook secrets that may be exposed. 2. Implement signature verification immediately. 3. Test with both valid and invalid signatures. 4. Monitor logs for unauthorized webhook attempts.

findings.title: Hardcoded credentials in docker-compose.yml
findings.description: docker-compose.yml contains hardcoded database credentials and Redis URL in the environment section for the 'api' service (line 6: DATABASE_URL=postgresql://webhookuser:webhookpass@postgres:5432/webhookdb). It also contains POSTGRES_USER and POSTGRES_PASSWORD environment variables (lines 54-55). While these are for local dev, they are committed to the repository and could be used to access databases if network isolation fails.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker clones the public repository or searches GitHub for the exposed credentials. 2. If the PostgreSQL port is exposed (misconfigured firewall, staging env), attacker connects using webhookuser:webhookpass@postgres:5432/webhookdb. 3. Attacker dumps the webhook_events table, potentially accessing sensitive webhook payloads (payment data, GitHub tokens, etc.). 4. Attacker could modify/delete webhook data or inject malicious data.
findings.impact: Full database compromise. Webhook payloads often contain sensitive data (payment details, authentication tokens, PII). An attacker with database access can read, modify, or delete this data. If the same credentials are reused elsewhere, the blast radius increases. PostgreSQL running in Docker may have network exposure in certain configurations.
findings.recommendation: 1. Remove hardcoded credentials from docker-compose.yml immediately. 2. Use environment variables with defaults: DATABASE_URL=${DATABASE_URL:-postgresql://user:pass@postgres:5432/db}. 3. Ensure .env is in .gitignore. 4. Rotate the webhookpass password. 5. Use a secrets manager (Docker secrets, Vault) for production.
findings.playbook: 1. Revoke the credential: docker exec -it hookrelay-postgres-1 psql -U webhookuser -d webhookdb -c "ALTER USER webhookuser WITH PASSWORD 'new_secure_password';" 2. Update docker-compose.yml to use env vars. 3. git add docker-compose.yml && git commit -m "security: remove hardcoded credentials" 4. Force-push if history contains the old credentials, use git filter-branch to scrub history.

findings.title: .env file NOT in .gitignore
findings.description: .env file exists in the repository root, but .gitignore does NOT contain a rule to ignore .env files. The .env.example file shows that .env should contain sensitive data (CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_TOKEN, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET). If .env is ever committed, these secrets will be exposed in git history.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Developer accidentally commits .env file (happens frequently). 2. Attacker finds the commit in git history (even if later deleted, git log still contains it). 3. Attacker extracts Cloudflare tunnel token, GitHub tokens, webhook secrets. 4. With GitHub token, attacker can access private repos, modify webhooks, access organization data. With Cloudflare token, attacker can reconfigure tunnels or access analytics.
findings.impact: Full compromise of Cloudflare tunnel and GitHub integrations. Attackers can read/update webhooks, access private repositories, and potentially pivot to other systems using the compromised tokens. If the repo is public, this is immediately exploitable by anyone.
findings.recommendation: 1. Add '.env' and '.env.*' to .gitignore immediately. 2. Check if .env was ever committed: git log --all --full-history -- .env. 3. If committed, rotate ALL secrets and scrub history with git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner.
findings.playbook: 1. echo '.env' >> .gitignore && echo '.env.*' >> .gitignore. 2. git add .gitignore && git commit -m "security: add .env to .gitignore". 3. Check for accidental commits: git log --all --full-history -- .env. 4. If found, rotate secrets and scrub: git filter-branch --index-filter 'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch .env' HEAD.

findings.title: package-lock.json missing for frontend
findings.description: The frontend directory does not have a package-lock.json file (npm audit failed with 'ENOLOCK' error). Lockfiles ensure reproducible builds and protect against supply chain attacks where attackers publish malicious versions of dependencies with patch versions.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises a dependency (e.g., react-dom) by publishing a malicious version with the same minor version but malicious code. 2. Without a lockfile, npm install picks up the malicious version. 3. Malicious code executes in the browser when user visits the HookRelay dashboard, potentially stealing session data, injecting malicious scripts, or exfiltrating webhook data.
findings.impact: Supply chain attack via compromised npm packages. The frontend is a React dashboard that handles webhook data - compromised packages could exfiltrate sensitive payloads or inject malicious JavaScript. Developers' machines could also be compromised during npm install.
findings.recommendation: 1. Run 'npm install' in frontend/ to generate package-lock.json. 2. Commit the lockfile to ensure reproducible builds: git add frontend/package-lock.json && git commit -m "build: add missing package-lock.json". 3. Consider using npm ci instead of npm install in CI/CD for reproducible builds.
findings.playbook: 1. cd frontend && npm install. 2. git add package-lock.json && git commit -m "Fix: add missing package-lock.json". 3. Enable npm audit in CI: npm audit --production.

findings.title: Dockerfiles missing USER directive (run as root)
findings.description: All three Dockerfiles (backend, frontend, tunnel) do not have a USER directive, meaning they run as root inside the container. While this is a dev environment, if any container processes external input (like the webhook handler), a container breakout would give attacker root access on the host.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker finds a vulnerability in the FastAPI app or nginx (e.g., path traversal, RCE). 2. Attacker escapes the container using a Docker breakout technique. 3. Since the container runs as root, the attacker gains root access to the host system. 4. Attacker can access other containers, read all environment variables, access Docker socket if mounted.
findings.impact: Container breakout leads to host root compromise. While this is primarily a dev environment, if the same pattern is copied to production, the risk is severe. Root containers also violate least-privilege principles and may interfere with other system services.
findings.recommendation: Add USER directive to all Dockerfiles. Create a non-root user: RUN adduser -D appuser && chown -R appuser /app && USER appuser. For the backend, ensure the app can still bind to port 8000 (may need to run as root initially, then drop privileges).
findings.playbook: 1. Add to each Dockerfile before CMD: RUN adduser -D appuser && chown -R appuser /app. 2. Add: USER appuser. 3. Test that the app still works: docker compose up --build.

findings.title: node_modules EXISTS in frontend directory
findings.description: The frontend/node_modules directory exists, indicating it may have been committed to the repository. node_modules should never be committed as it contains platform-specific binaries and makes the repo massive. It also contains dependencies that should be resolved via package.json and lockfile.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. If node_modules is committed, the repo size becomes huge. 2. Developers may accidentally use the committed node_modules instead of running npm install. 3. Committed node_modules may contain outdated or vulnerable dependencies that don't match package.json. 4. Supply chain attack: if attacker compromises the repo, they could inject malicious code into node_modules.
findings.impact: Repository bloat, potential supply chain issues, and developer confusion. While not directly exploitable, it indicates poor dependency management practices that often accompany other security issues.
findings.recommendation: 1. Ensure node_modules is in .gitignore: echo 'node_modules/' >> frontend/.gitignore. 2. If committed, remove: git rm -r --cached frontend/node_modules && git commit -m "Fix: remove committed node_modules".
findings.playbook: 1. Check: git ls-files node_modules. 2. If tracked: git rm -r --cached frontend/node_modules. 3. Add node_modules/ to frontend/.gitignore. 4. Commit: git add .gitignore && git commit -m "Fix: ignore node_modules".

owasp_assessment.A02_Cryptographic_Failures: LOW - No hardcoded cryptographic secrets found, but webhook signatures not verified (Finding #1)
owasp_assessment.A03_Injection: MEDIUM - SQL injection possible if SQLAlchemy not properly parameterized (code review needed), but ORM typically handles this
owasp_assessment.A04_Insecure_Design: HIGH - Webhook design lacking signature verification is a fundamental design flaw (Finding #1)
owasp_assessment.A05_Security_Misconfiguration: CRITICAL - Hardcoded credentials (Finding #2), .env not in gitignore (Finding #3), Docker runs as root (Finding #5)
owasp_assessment.A06_Vulnerable_Components: MEDIUM - Missing package-lock.json (Finding #4) increases supply chain risk
owasp_assessment.A07_Identification_Authentication_Failur: HIGH - Webhook endpoints have no authentication/signature verification (Finding #1)
owasp_assessment.A08_Software_Data_Integrity_Failures: LOW - No CI/CD pipeline found to assess
owasp_assessment.A09_Security_Logging_Monitoring_Failures: MEDIUM - Webhook events logged to DB but no security event logging found
